extracted.intended_audience: health researchers, manuscript authors, journal editors, and guideline developers
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining what a reporting guideline is and what features/requirements such guidelines should have to guide authors in reporting health research. Covers purposes, acceptable forms, core features, and examples by study type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guideline — formal definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “A checklist, flow diagram, or structured text to guide authors in reporting a specific type of research, developed using explicit methodology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the EQUATOR Network's working definition of a reporting guideline; it emphasizes both form (checklist/flow diagram/structured text) and that the guideline must be developed using explicit methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purposes of a reporting guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline provides a minimum list of information needed to ensure a manuscript can be, for example: Understood by a reader, Replicated by a researcher, Used by a doctor to make a clinical decision, and Included in a systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four intended uses articulate the essential outcomes that reporting guidelines aim to achieve for manuscripts: clarity, reproducibility, clinical utility, and inclusion in evidence syntheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable forms of a reporting guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether presented as structured text or a checklist, a reporting guideline is a checklist, flow diagram, or structured text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly lists checklist, flow diagram, and structured text as valid presentation formats for reporting guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core features required of a reporting guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline presents a clear list of reporting items that should appear in a paper and explains how the list was developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two linked requirements: (1) provide a clear, minimum list of items authors should report; (2) document and explain the methodology/process by which that list was created (transparency of development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of reporting guidelines by study type
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines exist for main study types (examples listed): Randomised trials (CONSORT + extensions); Observational studies (STROBE + extensions); Systematic reviews (PRISMA + extensions); Study protocols (SPIRIT, PRISMA-P); Diagnostic/prognostic studies (STARD, TRIPOD); Case reports (CARE + extensions); Clinical practice guidelines (AGREE, RIGHT); Qualitative research (SRQR, COREQ); Animal pre-clinical studies (ARRIVE); Quality improvement studies (SQUIRE + extensions); Economic evaluations (CHEERS + extensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists major, canonical reporting guidelines mapped to study types as examples of the kinds of guidelines that satisfy the definition and features above. These serve as model templates authors can consult for specific study designs.
